etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle French indispensable, from Medieval Latin indispensābilis, corresponding to in- +‎ dispensable.

definitions.definition: (ecclesiastical, obsolete) Not admitting ecclesiastical dispensation; not subject to release or exemption; that cannot be allowed by bending the canonical rules. [16th–17th c.]
(of duties, rules etc.) Unbendable, that cannot be set aside or ignored. [from 17th c.]

quote.citation: 1679–1715, Gilbert Burnet, “(please specify the page)”, in The History of the Reformation of the Church of England., London:  […]  T[homas] H[odgkin] for Richard Chiswell, […]:
quote.text: The law was moral and indispensable.

definitions.definition: Absolutely necessary or requisite; that one cannot do without. [from 17th c.]

quote.citation: 2006, Edwin Black, chapter 2, in Internal Combustion‎[1]:
quote.text: But through the oligopoly, charcoal fuel proliferated throughout London's trades and industries. By the 1200s, brewers and bakers, tilemakers, glassblowers, pottery producers, and a range of other craftsmen all became hour-to-hour consumers of charcoal. This only magnified the indispensable nature of the oligopolists.
And my friends in politics, no-one is remotely indispensable and our brilliant and Darwinian system will produce another leader, equally committed to taking this country forward through tough times.

definitions.definition: A thing that is not dispensable; a necessity. [from 17th c.]
(in the plural, colloquial, dated) Trousers. [from 19th c.]
